verse.text: In many parts and in many ways God spoke long ago to the ancestors by the prophets;

note.traditional: at many times (KJV: at sundry times)

verse.note: The Greek adverb means 'in many portions' or 'piece by piece', not 'on many occasions'. The point is that the earlier revelation came in fragments, in contrast to the single, complete word spoken in the Son. Several modern commentators and some translations render it this way. The two opening adverbs both begin with poly-, which 'many ... many' echoes.

verse.text: at the end of these days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, and through whom he also made the ages.

note.term: at the end of these days

verse.note: The Greek adapts a Septuagint idiom for 'in the latter days' by adding 'these': literally 'at the last of these days'. The author is saying that the present period has reached its close with the coming of the Son. 'In these last days' is the usual English and conveys much the same thought less exactly.

The Greek word is a plural of the ordinary word for an age or long era. In Jewish Greek it could refer to the whole created order viewed as a succession of ages, and most translations and lexicons render it 'the worlds' or 'the universe' here and at 11:3. 'The ages' keeps the temporal colouring and the link with 'forever' (literally 'to the age') in verse 8. The created universe is certainly included in the meaning.

verse.text: He is the radiance of God’s glory and the imprint of his being, and he sustains all things by his powerful word. When he had through himself made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,
verse.note: The word can mean light shining out from a source (radiance) or light thrown back from a surface (reflection). Most ancient Greek commentators and most modern translations take it in the first sense, as here; a minority prefer 'reflection'. The same word describes Wisdom in Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, which the author probably has in mind.

note.traditional: the express image of his person / the exact representation of his being

verse.note: The first Greek noun was used for the mark stamped by a die or seal, as on a coin, which reproduces the original exactly. The second (hypostasis) here means underlying reality or essential being. It later became a technical term in debates about the Trinity, but that sense should not be read back into this verse; the King James rendering 'person' reflects that later usage.

note.traditional: by the word of his power, when he had made purification

verse.note: Manuscripts differ here. Many, followed by most modern translations, read 'by the word of his power' and have no 'through himself' in the next clause. The edition translated here has no 'his' with 'power' in the Greek (the 'his' in 'his powerful word' is supplied for English) and reads 'through himself' with the purification clause. Other manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, have both. The sense is little changed.

verse.text: having become as far superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.
For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son; today I have fathered you”? Or again, “I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me”?
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for a father producing a child. 'Begotten' is accurate but archaic; 'fathered' says the same thing in current English. The quotation is Psalm 2:7, a royal psalm in which God declares the king his son at his enthronement. The second quotation is God's promise to David about his heir in 2 Samuel 7:14.

verse.text: And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “And let all God’s angels worship him.”
verse.note: The word 'again' may simply introduce another quotation, as in verse 5, or it may belong with the verb: 'when he again brings the firstborn into the world', pointing to Christ's return. The Greek word order slightly favours the second reading, and some translations and commentators adopt it. Most translations take it as a quotation marker, as here. When the 'bringing in' takes place (incarnation, exaltation or return) is also disputed.

note.term: let all God’s angels worship him

verse.note: The quotation follows the Greek version of Deuteronomy 32:43, which is longer than the traditional Hebrew text; a similar line appears in Psalm 97:7. The line is therefore missing from most English Old Testaments, which follow the Hebrew. A Hebrew manuscript of Deuteronomy among the Dead Sea Scrolls supports the longer form.

verse.text: Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.”
verse.note: The Greek word means both 'wind' and 'spirit'. In this quotation of Psalm 104:4, paired with 'a flame of fire', it is taken as 'winds': angels are changeable servants, like the elements, in contrast to the Son whose throne is permanent. The same word is translated 'spirits' in verse 14, and the author may intend the echo.

verse.text: But of the Son: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, and the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.
verse.note: The Greek of this quotation from Psalm 45:6–7 can also be read 'God is your throne'. Most translators and commentators take 'God' as an address to the Son, which suits the author's argument and is how the Greek psalm is usually understood. Some manuscripts read 'his kingdom' instead of 'your kingdom' at the end of the verse, which would favour the alternative reading. In verse 9, 'God, your God' could likewise be read 'O God, your God'.

text.q: You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”

verse.note: The Greek word is built on the word for 'law' and denotes conduct that disregards God's law. 'Wickedness' and 'iniquity' are the usual renderings and are not wrong, but 'lawlessness' is closer to what the word says and makes a sharper contrast with 'righteousness'.

verse.text: And: “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the works of your hands.
verse.note: The Greek is plural and refers here to the created heavens paired with the earth, not to God's dwelling or simply the visible sky. The singular 'heaven' would suggest God's dwelling and 'the skies' would be too narrow for something said to perish and be rolled up, so the plural 'the heavens' is kept. The quotation is Psalm 102:25–27, addressed in the psalm to the Lord God and here applied to the Son.

text.q: They will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment,
and like a cloak you will roll them up; like a garment they too will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will never run out.”

verse.text: But to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”?
Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service for the sake of those who are going to inherit salvation?
For this reason we must pay all the more attention to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away.
For if the message spoken through angels proved firm, and every transgression and act of disobedience received its just repayment,
verse.note: This is the Law given at Sinai. Jewish tradition of the period held that angels were present and acted as intermediaries when the Law was given, an idea also reflected in Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if that message was binding, the one delivered by the Lord himself is more so.

verse.text: how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? It was first spoken through the Lord and was confirmed to us by those who heard him,
while God added his own testimony with signs and wonders and various acts of power, and with distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will.
For it was not to angels that he subjected the world to come, about which we are speaking.
But someone has testified somewhere, saying, “What is a human being that you remember him, or a son of man that you care for him?
verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 8:4–6 in its Greek form. The Greek word means a human being rather than a male, and 'son of man' in the parallel line is a Semitic idiom for the same thing. The singular 'him' is kept because the author goes on to apply the psalm to Jesus; whether 'him' in verse 8 still means humanity in general or already means Jesus is disputed.

text.q: You made him for a little while lower than angels; you crowned him with glory and honor;

verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean 'a little' in degree or 'for a little while' in time. The Hebrew psalm means degree, but the Greek allows either, and the use made of the phrase in verse 9, where Jesus' lowering is followed by his crowning, favours the temporal sense. Translations are divided.

note.term: you crowned him with glory and honor

verse.note: Many manuscripts add a further line from the psalm here, 'and set him over the works of your hands'. The Greek edition translated here treats it as a later addition by copyists completing the quotation, and omits it.

verse.text: you subjected all things under his feet.” For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him. But as it is, we do not yet see all things subjected to him.

But we do see the one who for a little while was made lower than angels, Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that apart from God he might taste death for everyone.
verse.note: Nearly all manuscripts read 'by the grace of God' (chariti theou), and almost every English translation follows them. The Greek edition translated here adopts 'apart from God' (chōris theou), found in very few manuscripts but known to early Christian writers including Origen, on the ground that copyists were more likely to soften the harder reading than to create it. If original, it probably means that Jesus died in abandonment by God, or possibly that he died for everyone except God. The majority of scholars still prefer 'by the grace of God'.

verse.text: For it was fitting that he, for whom all things exist and through whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should perfect the pioneer of their salvation through sufferings.
verse.note: The word describes someone who begins something and leads others into it: the founder of a city, the head of a clan, a leader who goes first. English versions vary between 'author', 'founder', 'captain' and 'pioneer'. 'Pioneer' is chosen because the context is of one who goes ahead on a path along which many others are brought to glory.

The verb means to bring something to its goal or completion, and does not imply an earlier moral defect. In the Greek Old Testament a related expression is used for installing a priest in office, and many scholars hear that overtone here: through suffering Jesus was fully fitted for his role as high priest.

verse.text: For the one who makes holy and those who are being made holy are all from one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers,
verse.note: The Greek says only 'from one', without a noun. It may mean one Father, that is God, which is the most common view, or one human ancestor such as Adam or Abraham, or one shared human stock. The rendering leaves the reference open.

verse.text: saying, “I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise.”

note.term: I will proclaim your name to my brothers

verse.note: The author places three Scripture texts on Jesus' lips: Psalm 22:22 here, and Isaiah 8:17 and 8:18 in the next verse, all in their Greek form. Psalm 22 is the psalm of the righteous sufferer whose opening line Jesus cries from the cross in the Gospels. The quotations are cited to show the Son identifying himself with God's people as family.

This is the word usually translated 'church' elsewhere in the New Testament. In the psalm being quoted it is the Greek Old Testament's term for Israel gathered for worship, and a first-century hearer also knew it as an ordinary word for a civic gathering. This translation uses 'assembly' throughout so that the reader can see it is one word. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering elsewhere, though many versions also use 'assembly' or 'congregation' in this verse.

verse.text: And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Here I am, and the children God has given me.”

Since, then, the children share in blood and flesh, he too in the same way took part in the same things, so that through death he might render powerless the one who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,
and set free those who all their lives were held in slavery by fear of death.
For surely it is not angels that he takes hold of; it is the offspring of Abraham that he takes hold of.
verse.note: The verb means to take hold of or grasp. Most modern translations render it 'helps', taking the grasp as one of rescue; older interpreters, followed by the King James Version, understood it as taking on a nature, that is, the incarnation. The literal sense is kept here because it covers both and because the same verb describes God taking Israel by the hand in the passage quoted at Hebrews 8:9.

verse.text: That is why he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in matters relating to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people.

note.traditional: to make propitiation for; to make reconciliation for

verse.note: Whether this verb means turning away God's wrath ('propitiation') or removing sin ('expiation') is a long-running dispute. Here its direct object is 'sins', which fits the removal of sin more naturally, though many scholars hold that averting wrath is still implied. 'Make atonement' is the sacrificial term that covers both and matches the word's use in the Greek Old Testament.

verse.text: For because he himself has suffered when tested, he is able to help those who are being tested.
verse.note: The Greek verb covers both testing and tempting, and most English versions have 'tempted' here. 'Tested' is chosen because the context is trial through suffering, which presses a person to abandon faithfulness, rather than enticement to particular sins. The two ideas overlap and the traditional rendering is defensible.

verse.text: Therefore, holy brothers and sisters, sharers in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession,
verse.note: This is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called an apostle. The word means someone sent with a commission, an envoy. Here it presents Jesus as the one sent by God, paired with his role as high priest representing the people to God.

verse.text: who was faithful to the one who appointed him, just as Moses also was in his house.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for 'make' and could be read as 'the one who made him'. Most translators take it as 'appointed', a sense it has in the Septuagint (for example of God 'making' Moses and Aaron in 1 Samuel 12:6), and that fits the context of office and faithfulness.

The wording echoes Numbers 12:7, where God says of Moses, 'he is faithful in all my house'. 'His house' is therefore God's house, meaning God's household or people, not Moses' own. The argument that follows plays on 'house' as both a building and a household.

verse.text: For he has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, to the same degree that the builder of a house has greater honor than the house.
For every house is built by someone, but the one who built everything is God.
Now Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant, as a witness to the things that would be spoken later,
verse.note: The Greek word, used only here in the New Testament, is taken from the Septuagint of Numbers 12:7. It is not the common word for a slave but a more dignified term for a personal attendant who serves freely. The contrast with Christ is therefore between an honoured attendant in the household and the son set over it.

verse.text: but Christ was faithful as a son over his house. We are his house, if we hold fast our confidence and the hope in which we boast.

note.term: the hope in which we boast
note.traditional: the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end

verse.note: Many manuscripts add 'firm to the end' after these words, and older English versions include it. The phrase is absent from some of the earliest witnesses and was probably copied in from verse 14, where it is original. SBLGNT omits it.

verse.text: Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear his voice,

text.q: do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, as on the day of testing in the wilderness,

verse.note: The quotation in verses 7–11 is Psalm 95:7–11 in its Greek form. Where the Hebrew psalm names the places Meribah and Massah (Exodus 17:1–7), the Greek version translates the names as 'rebellion' and 'testing'. The related verb in verse 16 is rendered 'rebelled' to keep the link.

text.q: where your ancestors tested me, putting me to the proof, and saw my works
for forty years. That is why I was disgusted with this generation and said, ‘They always go astray in their hearts, and they have not known my ways.’

verse.note: In the psalm itself the forty years belong with what follows: God was displeased with that generation for forty years. The wording here, with 'that is why' inserted after the phrase, attaches the forty years to seeing God's works. The author knows the other division too and uses it in verse 17.

note.traditional: I was angry with / I was grieved with / I was provoked with

verse.note: Most translations have 'angry' or 'provoked'. In the Septuagint, which is nearly the only place the verb is found, it regularly translates Hebrew words for loathing or being repelled by something. 'Disgusted' reflects that usage and keeps the verb distinct from the ordinary word for anger in verse 11.

text.q: So I swore in my anger, ‘They shall never enter my rest.’”

note.term: They shall never enter my rest
note.traditional: They shall not enter into my rest

verse.note: The Greek reads literally 'if they shall enter my rest', a Hebrew oath formula with the penalty clause left unspoken ('may such-and-such happen to me if...'). It amounts to an emphatic denial. In the psalm the 'rest' is the promised land, which the exodus generation was barred from entering (Numbers 14:20–35); the next chapter develops a larger meaning.

verse.text: See to it, brothers and sisters, that none of you has an evil heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God.
verse.note: The Greek word is the negative of the word translated 'faithful' in verses 2 and 5, and can mean either lack of trust or lack of faithfulness. 'Unbelief' follows the Numbers 14 background, where the people refuse to trust God's promise. The sense of disloyalty is also in view, as 'turns away' and the 'disobeyed' of verse 18 show.

verse.text: Instead, encourage one another every day, as long as it is called “Today,” so that none of you is hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
For we have become sharers in Christ, if indeed we hold fast our first resolve, firm to the end.
verse.note: The phrase can mean those who share in Christ, participating in him and what he gives, or those who share with Christ, his partners or companions. The same word clearly means 'companions' in 1:9, but takes the sense 'sharers in' at 3:1 and 6:4. Translations and commentators are divided.

note.traditional: our original confidence / the beginning of our confidence

verse.note: Most translations render this 'confidence' or 'assurance'. Lexicographers have questioned whether the word has that subjective sense in this period. Its attested meanings include 'underlying reality' (as in 1:3) and, in Hellenistic historians, a firm stand or steadfast resolve. The latter fits the call to hold firm here. Others take it as 'the reality we began with', and 'confidence' remains the majority rendering.

verse.text: As it is said: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.”
For who were they who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not all those who came out of Egypt led by Moses?

note.term: who were they who heard and yet rebelled
note.traditional: For some, when they had heard, did provoke: howbeit not all that came out of Egypt by Moses

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts had no accents, and the first word can be read as 'who?' or as 'some'. The King James Version took it as 'some' and made the verse a statement. Nearly all modern editors and translators read a question, matching the two parallel questions in verses 17 and 18.

verse.text: And with whom was he disgusted for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose corpses fell in the wilderness?
And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, if not to those who disobeyed?
So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.
Therefore, while a promise of entering his rest still remains, let us be afraid that any one of you should be found to have fallen short of it.
verse.note: The Greek verb can mean 'seem' or 'think', or 'be judged, be found'. The rendering takes it in the last sense, as a warning about an actual verdict. Others read it as a softened expression ('should seem to have fallen short') or as 'should think he has come too late' for the promise.

verse.text: For we too have had good news proclaimed to us, just as they did; but the word they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united in faith with those who listened.

note.term: they were not united in faith with those who listened
note.traditional: not being mixed with faith in them that heard it

verse.note: The manuscripts differ by one letter. The reading translated here, which has the stronger manuscript support, says that the wilderness generation was not joined in faith to those who truly listened. The other reading says the word itself was not combined with faith in its hearers, and older English versions follow it. The general point is the same on either reading.

verse.text: For we who have believed are entering that rest, just as he has said, “As I swore in my anger, ‘They shall never enter my rest,’” even though his works were finished from the foundation of the world.

note.term: They shall never enter my rest
note.traditional: They shall not enter my rest

verse.note: The Greek literally reads 'If they shall enter my rest', reproducing a Hebrew oath formula in which the penalty clause is left unspoken ('may such-and-such happen if...'). It functions as an emphatic denial. The quotation is from Psalm 95 in its Greek form, already cited in the previous chapter.

verse.text: For somewhere he has spoken about the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works,”
and again in this passage: “They shall never enter my rest.”
Since, then, it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly had the good news proclaimed to them did not enter because of disobedience,
he again appoints a certain day, “Today,” saying through David after so long a time, in the words already quoted, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”
For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken afterward about another day.
verse.note: In Greek the names Joshua and Jesus are identical. The context, leading Israel into the land, shows that Joshua son of Nun is meant, but a Greek reader would have heard the shared name, and the author may intend the contrast between the first Joshua and Jesus.

verse.text: So then, a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God;
verse.note: The author here switches from the word for 'rest' used throughout the chapter to a different and rare word meaning Sabbath observance, not attested in surviving Greek before this passage. It ties the promised rest to God's own rest on the seventh day, cited in verse 4.

verse.text: for the one who has entered God’s rest has also rested from his own works, just as God did from his.
verse.note: Most interpreters take this as a general statement about any believer who enters God's rest. A minority read it as referring specifically to Christ, who has finished his work and entered that rest ahead of his people. The Greek allows either.

verse.text: Let us therefore make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by following the same example of disobedience.

For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
And no creature is hidden from his sight, but everything is naked and laid bare to the eyes of the one to whom we must give account.
verse.note: The verb is formed from the word for 'neck' and its exact image here is uncertain. Suggestions include a wrestler gripping an opponent's neck or the bending back of a sacrificial victim's neck to expose the throat. The general sense of being exposed and defenceless is not in doubt.

note.term: to whom we must give account
note.traditional: with whom we have to do

verse.note: The Greek is terse: literally 'toward whom for us the word'. It can mean 'to whom we must render account' or more loosely 'with whom we have to deal'. The word translated 'account' is the same one translated 'word' in verse 12, so the passage opens and closes with the same term.

verse.text: Since, then, we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession.
verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that this translation keeps wherever God's dwelling is in view. Many English versions also keep the plural in this verse, though some flatten it to 'heaven'.

verse.text: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tested in every way just as we are, yet without sin.
verse.note: The Greek verb covers both testing and tempting; English must choose. 'Tested' is used here because the surrounding argument concerns Israel's testing in the wilderness and endurance under trial, and several modern versions do the same. 'Tempted' remains the more common rendering and is not wrong, since the trial includes the pull toward sin, as 'yet without sin' implies.

verse.text: Let us then approach the throne of grace with boldness, so that we may receive mercy and find grace for help at the right time.
For every high priest, taken from among people, is appointed on behalf of people in matters relating to God, to offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins.
He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, since he himself is also beset by weakness,
verse.note: The verb means to keep one's feelings within measure, and in period usage especially to hold anger in check. It is a cooler word than the 'sympathize' used of Jesus in 4:15: the ordinary high priest restrains his severity toward sinners because he shares their weakness. 'Ignorant and going astray' echoes the Law's category of unintentional sins, for which sacrifice was provided.

verse.text: and because of it he is obliged to offer sacrifice for sins, as for the people, so also for himself.
verse.note: On the Day of Atonement the high priest first offered a bull for his own sins and those of his household before offering for the people (Leviticus 16). The author will later contrast this with Jesus, who had no sin of his own to offer for.

verse.text: And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron also was.
So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest; it was the one who said to him, “You are my Son; today I have become your father,”

note.term: today I have become your father

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 2:7, where God addresses Israel's king at his enthronement. 'Begotten' is the long-standing English rendering, but the word is now archaic. Several modern versions give the same sense with 'become your father'. The Greek verb is the ordinary one for a father producing a child.

verse.text: just as he also says in another place, “You are a priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek.”
verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:4. The Greek word can mean a rank or class, or more loosely a kind or manner. Many scholars think the sense here is 'of the same kind as Melchizedek', since the author later paraphrases it as 'in the likeness of Melchizedek' (7:15). 'Order' should not suggest a succession of priests, because Melchizedek has no predecessors or successors in Scripture.

verse.text: In the days of his flesh he offered prayers and pleas, with a loud cry and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.

note.traditional: in that he feared; because of his reverent submission

verse.note: The Greek word can mean reverent awe before God or, less often, anxiety and dread. Most interpreters take it as 'heard because of his reverence'. A minority read 'heard and delivered from his dread'. The scene is usually connected with Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, though the author does not say so.

verse.text: Son though he was, he learned obedience from what he suffered,

note.term: learned obedience from what he suffered

verse.note: The Greek rhymes: emathen ('he learned') and epathen ('he suffered'). The pairing was a familiar saying in Greek literature, that suffering teaches. The author applies the commonplace to the Son, who might have been expected to be exempt from it.

verse.text: and, having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him,
verse.note: The verb means to bring something to its goal or completion. In Hebrews it describes Jesus being fully fitted for his priestly role through suffering and exaltation, not the removal of a moral flaw, which 4:15 rules out. In the Greek Old Testament the same word-family is used for the consecration of priests, and some scholars hear that overtone here.

verse.text: designated by God high priest in the order of Melchizedek.
About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become sluggish in hearing.
verse.note: The Greek pronoun can be masculine ('about him', meaning Melchizedek or Christ) or neuter ('about this', meaning the subject of Christ's priesthood). Either fits the context, and translations are divided.

verse.text: For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you the first elements of God’s oracles; you have come to need milk, not solid food.

note.traditional: that one teach you; someone to teach you

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts were written without accents, and the Greek word here can be accented to mean either 'someone' or 'what'. The second reading gives 'you need to be taught what the first elements are'. The edition translated here prints the first, and the difference in meaning is slight.

verse.text: For everyone who lives on milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, since that person is an infant.
verse.note: The phrase can mean teaching about righteousness, the Christian message as a whole, or reasoning about what is right, which would suit the next verse's 'distinguish good from evil'. Some also see an idiom for mature, properly formed speech, in contrast to an infant's. The literal rendering is kept because the Greek does not settle the question.

verse.text: But solid food is for the mature, those who because of their mature state have their faculties trained to distinguish good from evil.

note.traditional: by reason of use; by constant practice

verse.note: English versions have long rendered this word as 'practice' or 'use', as though the mature became so by exercise. In Greek of the period, however, the word regularly means a state or condition of body or mind, the result of training and not the process. Lexical study in recent decades has favored that sense here, and recent lexicons give 'state of maturity'. The idea of training is carried by the next phrase, 'faculties trained'.

verse.text: Therefore, leaving behind the elementary message about Christ, let us move on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of turning back from dead works and of faith in God,
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'repentance', which most translations keep as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English 'repent' centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction. Here the turn is away from 'dead works' and is paired with faith directed toward God.

Literally 'the word of the beginning of Christ'. The phrase can mean the basic teaching about Christ, as rendered here, or the teaching Christ himself first gave. Most interpreters take it the first way, in line with 'the basic elements' mentioned in 5:12.

verse.text: instruction about washings and the laying on of hands, about the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment.
verse.note: The manuscripts differ by one letter. The reading followed here, found in some of the earliest witnesses, makes 'instruction' a description of the foundation itself. Most manuscripts and many editions read 'of instruction', which makes it one more item in the list of what the foundation consists of. The overall sense is little affected.

Many translations have 'baptisms', though several recent ones have 'washings' or 'cleansing rites'. The word is plural and is not the usual New Testament term for Christian baptism; elsewhere it refers to ritual washings (Hebrews 9:10; Mark 7:4). It probably covers teaching that distinguished Christian baptism from other Jewish washings, but exactly what is meant is uncertain.

verse.text: And this we will do, if indeed God permits.
For it is impossible, when people have once been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift and come to share in the Holy Spirit,
have tasted the goodness of God’s word and the powers of the coming age,
and then have fallen away, to renew them again to turning back, since they are crucifying the Son of God again for themselves and exposing him to public disgrace.

note.term: crucifying the Son of God again

verse.note: Outside the New Testament this verb regularly means simply 'crucify', with the prefix meaning 'up' rather than 'again'. Early Greek-speaking interpreters and the ancient versions nevertheless understood 'crucify again' here, which suits the context of renewing 'again', and most translations follow them. Some scholars prefer the plain 'crucify'.

The Greek has participles with no conjunction. Most take them as giving the reason ('since they are crucifying'). Some read them as marking time ('while they are crucifying'), which would limit the impossibility to the period in which the rejection continues. The scope of this warning has been debated since antiquity.

verse.text: For land that drinks the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is farmed, receives a share of blessing from God;
but if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and close to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.
But about you, dear friends, we are convinced of better things, things that belong to salvation, even though we speak this way.
For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love you showed for his name when you served the holy ones, as you still do.
verse.note: Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue.

verse.text: And we long for each of you to show the same eagerness toward the full assurance of hope right to the end,
so that you do not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
For when God made his promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself,
saying, “I will surely bless you and surely multiply you.”

note.term: I will surely bless you and surely multiply you.
note.traditional: Surely blessing I will bless thee, and multiplying I will multiply thee

verse.note: This quotes Genesis 22:17, spoken after Abraham's offering of Isaac, where God introduces the promise with 'By myself I have sworn'. The Greek opens with an oath formula and doubles each verb ('blessing I will bless'), a Hebrew idiom for emphasis that is rendered here by 'surely'.

verse.text: And so, after waiting patiently, Abraham obtained the promise.
For people swear by someone greater than themselves, and an oath given as confirmation puts an end to every dispute among them.
So when God wanted to show still more clearly to the heirs of the promise that his purpose was unchangeable, he guaranteed it with an oath,
so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to take hold of the hope set before us.
verse.note: The two things are generally understood to be God's promise and the oath he added to it. Under Israel's law a matter was established by two witnesses, and here God himself supplies both.

note.term: to take hold of the hope set before us
note.traditional: to lay hold upon the hope set before us

verse.note: The Greek can be construed in two ways: 'we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to take hold of the hope', or 'we who have fled to take hold of the hope might have strong encouragement'. The verb can also mean 'hold fast' to what one already has. The English word order leaves the first two options open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: We have this hope as an anchor of the soul, secure and firm, and it enters the inner place behind the curtain,

note.term: the inner place behind the curtain

verse.note: The curtain is the one that screened off the innermost room of the tabernacle and temple, the Most Holy Place. Only the high priest entered it, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The image prepares for the argument of chapters 7 to 10 that Jesus has entered God's presence itself as high priest.

verse.text: where Jesus has entered as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

note.term: according to the order of Melchizedek

verse.note: The wording comes from Psalm 110:4, 'You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek', already quoted in 5:6. Melchizedek is the priest-king of Salem who blessed Abraham in Genesis 14. The author returns here to the theme he broke off at 5:10 and develops it in chapter 7.

verse.text: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of God Most High, who met Abraham as he was returning from the defeat of the kings and blessed him,
and to whom Abraham apportioned a tenth of everything, is first, by the translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.

note.term: by the translation of his name

verse.note: The author explains two Hebrew terms for Greek readers. Melchizedek is taken as “my king is righteousness” or “king of righteousness,” and Salem is linked with the Hebrew word for peace, shalom. Such interpretation of names was a common practice among Jewish writers of the period.

verse.text: Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest in perpetuity.

note.term: Without father, without mother, without genealogy

verse.note: Genesis 14 introduces Melchizedek without naming his parents, his descent, his birth or his death, which is striking for a priest, since priestly office depended on recorded ancestry. The author reasons from this silence of Scripture: as he stands in the text, Melchizedek has no beginning or end. Most interpreters take this as an argument from the scriptural portrait rather than a claim that the historical figure was not a human being, though some think the author regarded him as a heavenly being.

verse.text: Consider how great this man is, to whom Abraham, the patriarch himself, gave a tenth from the best of the spoils.

Now those of the sons of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment according to the law to collect a tenth from the people, that is, from their brothers, even though these too have come from the loins of Abraham.
But the one whose genealogy is not traced from them has collected a tenth from Abraham and has blessed the one who had the promises.
And beyond all dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater.
Here, it is people who die that receive the tenth; there, it is one of whom it is testified that he lives.
And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who receives the tenth, has paid a tenth,
for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.

If, then, perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood—for on the basis of it the people received the law—what further need was there for a different priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be named according to the order of Aaron?
verse.note: The Greek word-family rendered “perfection” and “perfected” in this chapter (verses 11, 19, 28) means bringing something to its intended goal or completion, not moral flawlessness. In Hebrews the goal is full and lasting access to God, which the author says the old priesthood could not provide. In the Greek Old Testament the related verb is also used for installing a priest in office, and that sense may be heard in verse 28.

The Greek can mean that the law was given to the people on the basis of the Levitical priesthood, so that law and priesthood stand or fall together, or more loosely that the people received laws concerning it. The first reading fits the argument of verse 12 and is the one most interpreters adopt.

The phrase comes from Psalm 110:4. “Order” here does not mean a succession or society of priests, since Melchizedek had none; the word denotes a rank, kind or type, so the sense is “a priest of the Melchizedek kind.” The author himself paraphrases it in verse 15 as “in the likeness of Melchizedek.”

verse.text: For when the priesthood is changed, a change of law necessarily takes place as well.
For the one of whom these things are said belongs to a different tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar.
For it is evident that our Lord has sprung from Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priests.
verse.note: The verb is used of the sun or a star rising and of a plant sprouting. In the Greek Old Testament this language is attached to hopes for a coming ruler (the star rising out of Jacob in Numbers 24:17, and the related noun for the “Branch” in Zechariah). A first-century Jewish reader may well have heard a royal, messianic overtone, though the word can also simply mean descent.

verse.text: And it is more evident still if a different priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek,
one who has become a priest not according to a law of a commandment concerning the flesh but according to the power of an indestructible life.
verse.note: Literally “a commandment of flesh.” The adjective means made of or belonging to flesh, and here points to the rule that priests must come by physical descent from Levi, and perhaps also to the mortality of such priests, in contrast with “an indestructible life.” It does not carry the sense of sinfulness that “carnal” or “fleshly” suggests in English. Many modern versions paraphrase as “a requirement of bodily descent.”

verse.text: For it is testified: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”
For on the one hand a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness
(for the law perfected nothing), and on the other a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.
And inasmuch as this was not without an oath (for the others have become priests without an oath,
but he with an oath, through the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever’”),

note.traditional: Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec

verse.note: Many later manuscripts continue the quotation with “according to the order of Melchizedek,” as in verse 17, and the King James Version includes these words. Early and important witnesses lack them, and most editors judge that copyists completed the quotation from the psalm.

verse.text: to that same degree Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant.
And the others who have become priests are many in number, because death prevents them from remaining;
but he, because he remains forever, holds the priesthood permanently.
verse.note: The adjective describes the priesthood as permanent or inviolable. A long-standing alternative takes it to mean “not passing on to another,” that is, without successors, which suits the context well. The evidence of usage in the period favours “permanent,” and most lexicons adopt it. The practical difference is small.

verse.text: So he is also able to save completely those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can express degree (“completely, utterly”) or time (“for all time”). Both fit the context, since the argument turns on a priest who never dies, and the author may intend both. The rendering follows the more common sense of the phrase.

verse.text: For such a high priest was indeed fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and raised higher than the heavens.
He has no need, as the high priests do, to offer up sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins and then for those of the people (for this he did once for all when he offered up himself).
verse.note: The sequence of a sacrifice first for the high priest's own sins and then for the people's is prescribed in Leviticus 16 for the annual Day of Atonement, not for every day. The author may be combining this with the daily offerings of the sanctuary, or speaking broadly of the priests' unending round of sacrifice. Interpreters have not settled the point.

verse.text: For the law appoints as high priests people who have weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son, perfected forever.
Now the main point in what is being said is this: we have such a high priest, one who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens,
verse.note: The Greek word can mean either the chief point of an argument or a summary of it. Older versions took it as 'the sum' of what has been said. Most modern scholars prefer 'main point', since what follows advances the argument rather than recapping it.

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase for God's dwelling that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to the singular 'heaven'. The plural is kept here wherever the Greek has it.

verse.text: a minister of the sanctuary and of the true tent, which the Lord pitched, not a human being.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'of the holy', a plural that could in form mean 'holy ones' or 'holy things'. Hebrews regularly uses this neuter plural for the holy place of the sanctuary, and the pairing with 'tent' confirms that sense here. Nearly all interpreters agree.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a tent, and the Septuagint uses it for Israel's portable wilderness sanctuary. 'Tabernacle' comes from Latin and has become a technical religious term, hiding the plain image a Greek reader would have heard. Most English versions use 'tabernacle', though some use 'tent'.

verse.text: For every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices; so it is necessary for this one also to have something to offer.
Now if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are those who offer the gifts according to the law.

They serve what is a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, just as Moses was instructed when he was about to construct the tent. For he says, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain.”
verse.note: The verb was commonly used in this period for a divine communication or oracle, so the reader would understand that the instruction came from God. The quotation that follows is Exodus 25:40, where God tells Moses to build the wilderness sanctuary according to the pattern shown to him on Mount Sinai.

verse.text: But as it is, he has obtained a ministry that is superior to the same degree that the covenant he mediates is better, a covenant that has been enacted on better promises.
For if that first one had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second.
For finding fault with them he says: “Look, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will conclude a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,
verse.note: Manuscripts differ between two forms of 'them'. With one, the sense is 'finding fault with them, he says'. With the other, it could also be read 'finding fault, he says to them', which would make the fault lie with the covenant rather than the people. The translation follows the SBLGNT reading.

The quotation is Jeremiah 31:31–34 (38:31–34 in the Septuagint), the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament. Where the Septuagint has the usual verb for making a covenant, Hebrews has one meaning 'bring to completion'. Most versions render it 'make' or 'establish'; 'conclude' keeps the note of completion.

text.q: not like the covenant that I made with their ancestors on the day I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.

verse.note: Hebrews quotes Jeremiah in the Greek of the Septuagint. The Hebrew text of Jeremiah 31:32 reads differently at this point, usually translated 'though I was their husband' or 'their master'. English Old Testaments follow the Hebrew, which is why the two passages do not match.

text.q: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their mind and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.
And they will not teach, each one his fellow citizen and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.
For I will be merciful toward their wrongdoings, and their sins I will never remember again.”

verse.text: In saying “new,” he has made the first one old; and what is growing old and aging is close to disappearing.
verse.note: The same Greek verb appears twice in this verse, first for what God's word 'new' does to the first covenant and then for what is 'growing old'. Many modern translations use 'obsolete', which fits the argument but is narrower than the Greek and loses the simple contrast of new and old. 'Old' is used both times to keep the repetition.

verse.text: Now the first covenant had regulations for worship and the earthly holy place.
verse.note: The register's rendering for this word is 'righteous requirement', which suits Paul's usage. Here and in verse 10 the word has its common Septuagint sense of a statute or ordinance, namely the rules governing Israel's worship, and the author calls them 'regulations for the flesh' that were only temporary. 'Righteous requirements' would give them a moral weight the argument does not intend, so the usual 'regulations' is kept. The word 'covenant' is supplied in this verse, as in most translations; the Greek says only 'the first'.

verse.text: For a tent was set up, the first one, in which were the lampstand and the table and the presentation of the loaves; this is called the Holy Place.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent, and it is the Septuagint's term for Israel's wilderness sanctuary. 'Tabernacle' comes from the Latin for the same thing but now sounds like a special religious object. The author uses 'tent' both for the whole structure and for each of its two rooms, and his argument turns on that. Several modern translations also use 'tent'.

note.traditional: the showbread; the bread of the Presence

verse.note: The Greek phrase means the setting out of the loaves. It refers to the twelve loaves placed on the table before God each sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9). 'Bread of the Presence' renders the Hebrew name; the Greek expression used here is different and is translated as it stands.

verse.text: Behind the second curtain was a tent called the Holy of Holies,

which had a golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant, covered on all sides with gold. In the ark were a golden jar holding the manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant,

note.traditional: golden altar of incense (older versions: golden censer)

verse.note: The word can mean either a censer or an incense altar. Most scholars take it as the altar, as Jewish writers of the period used the word. Exodus places that altar in the outer room, just in front of the curtain. The author may be linking it to the inner room because of its use on the Day of Atonement, but the matter is debated.

verse.text: and above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the place of atonement. Of these things it is not possible to speak now in detail.
verse.note: In the Septuagint this word names the gold cover of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). 'Mercy seat' goes back to Tyndale and Luther and suggests a chair, which it was not. The same phrase is used for this word in Romans 3:25 so that the reader can see the connection, though the meaning there is disputed.

verse.text: With these things set up in this way, the priests go continually into the first tent, carrying out the acts of worship,
but into the second only the high priest goes, once a year, and not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the sins the people have committed in ignorance.
By this the Holy Spirit shows that the way into the holy place has not yet been revealed as long as the first tent still stands.
This is a symbol for the present time, in accordance with which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot make the worshipper perfect in conscience,
but deal only with foods and drinks and various washings, regulations for the flesh imposed until the time for setting things straight.
verse.note: As in verse 1, the word means a ritual ordinance, not a 'righteous requirement' in the moral sense. The author is stressing that these rules concerned the body only and were temporary.

verse.text: But when Christ arrived as high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent, not made by hands, that is, not of this creation,

note.term: the good things that have come

verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between 'the good things that have come' and 'the good things that are about to come'. The reading translated here has early and diverse support and is adopted by most modern editions. The other may have arisen under the influence of the similar phrase in 10:1.

verse.text: and not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, he entered the holy place once for all, obtaining eternal redemption.
For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled on those who have been defiled, make them holy so that their flesh is clean,
verse.note: Numbers 19 prescribes that a red heifer be burned and its ashes mixed with water. The mixture was sprinkled on anyone made ritually unclean by contact with a corpse. The uncleanness in view is ceremonial, a bar to taking part in worship; it is not moral guilt.

verse.text: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works so that we may worship the living God!
verse.note: The Greek has no article: 'through eternal spirit'. Most interpreters take it as the Holy Spirit. Others understand Christ's own spirit or his eternal nature, in contrast to animal offerings that perish. A few manuscripts read 'Holy Spirit', which shows how early readers understood it.

The verb is the one used throughout the chapter for the service of God in the sanctuary (verses 1, 6, 9). Most translations switch to 'serve' here. 'Worship' is kept so that the contrast shows: the old rites could not perfect the worshipper, but Christ's blood fits people for the worship of the living God.

verse.text: And for this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, a death having taken place for redemption from the transgressions committed under the first covenant, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.
For where there is a will, the death of the one who made it has to be established;
verse.note: The Greek word translated 'covenant' everywhere else in this chapter was also the everyday term for a last will and testament. Most translators think the author plays on that second sense in verses 16–17, prompted by 'inheritance' in verse 15, and that is followed here. A minority of scholars keep 'covenant' throughout and read these verses as referring to the death, represented by sacrificed animals, that ratified a covenant. English cannot reproduce the single word.

verse.text: for a will takes effect only at death, since it is never in force while the one who made it is alive.
That is why not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.

For when every commandment had been spoken by Moses to all the people according to the law, he took the blood of the calves, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the scroll itself and all the people,
saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded for you.”
And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in the service.
Indeed, according to the law almost everything is cleansed with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.
It was necessary, then, for the copies of the things in the heavens to be cleansed by these means, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these.

note.traditional: the heavenly things; the things in heaven

verse.note: The Greek is plural here, a Semitic way of speaking of God's dwelling, and the plural is kept. In verse 24 the word is singular and is translated 'heaven itself'. Most translations make no distinction.

verse.text: For Christ did not enter a holy place made by hands, a counterpart of the true one, but heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God on our behalf.
Nor did he enter to offer himself many times, as the high priest enters the holy place year after year with blood not his own;
otherwise he would have had to suffer many times since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has been revealed once, at the end of the ages, to do away with sin through his sacrifice.
And just as it is appointed for people to die once, and after that comes judgment,
so also Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who are eagerly waiting for him.

note.traditional: without sin; apart from sin; not to bear sin

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'apart from sin'. The contrast with the first appearing 'to bear the sins of many' (an echo of Isaiah 53:12) shows the sense: the second coming has nothing more to do with sin, which was dealt with once for all. The phrase does not mean Christ will then be sinless as though he had not been before.

verse.text: For since the law has a shadow of the good things to come and not the form itself of the realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that they offer perpetually year after year, make perfect those who draw near.
verse.note: The Greek word usually means 'image' or 'likeness', but here it is set against 'shadow' and denotes the real shape of the thing, not a copy of it. 'Image' would suggest to a modern reader a second kind of copy, which is the opposite of the point. Several recent translations likewise use 'true form'.

verse.text: Otherwise, would they not have stopped being offered, since the worshippers, cleansed once for all, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?
But in those sacrifices there is a reminder of sins year after year,
for it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
Therefore, when he comes into the world, he says: “Sacrifice and offering you did not want, but a body you prepared for me.

note.term: a body you prepared for me

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 40:6–8 in its Greek (Septuagint) form, which the author hears as words spoken by Christ on entering the world. The Hebrew text of the psalm reads 'ears you have dug for me' at this point; the author's argument in verse 10 depends on the Greek wording, 'a body'.

text.q: In whole burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure.
Then I said, ‘See, I have come—in the scroll of the book it is written about me—to do your will, O God.’”

verse.text: After saying above, “Sacrifices and offerings and whole burnt offerings and sin offerings you did not want, nor did you take pleasure in them,” these being offered according to the law,
he then said, “See, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second.
By that will we have been made holy through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
verse.note: The verb means to set apart as belonging to God, and it is the verbal form of the ordinary word 'holy'. 'Sanctified' is accurate but hides that connection and has acquired a specialised sense of gradual moral improvement that is not the point here. Some modern translations also use 'made holy'.

verse.text: And every priest stands day after day ministering and offering again and again the same sacrifices, which can never remove sins.
But this one, having offered a single sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down at the right hand of God,
verse.note: The phrase can be attached either to what precedes ('offered a single sacrifice for sins for all time') or to what follows ('sat down for all time at the right hand of God'). The Greek word order allows both and interpreters are divided. The rendering here takes it with the sacrifice, matching verse 14; the seated posture, in contrast to the priests who 'stand' in verse 11, makes the point of finished work on either reading.

verse.text: waiting from then on until his enemies are made a footstool for his feet,
for by a single offering he has made perfect for all time those who are being made holy.
The Holy Spirit also testifies to us, for after saying,

text.q: “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and I will write them on their minds,”

verse.text: he adds, “and their sins and their lawless acts I will remember no more.”
verse.note: The Greek has no words corresponding to 'he adds'; the sentence that begins 'after saying' in verse 15 is never formally completed. Most interpreters and translations take verse 17 as the point where it resumes and supply a phrase like this, as some later manuscripts also do. A minority take 'says the Lord' in verse 16 as the resumption. The quotation is from Jeremiah 31:33–34.

verse.text: Now where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
Therefore, brothers and sisters, since we have confidence for entry into the holy place by the blood of Jesus,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as fellow members of a family or community. 'Brothers' alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice.

The Greek is a plural, 'the holy things' or 'holy places', used in Hebrews for the sanctuary, and here for its innermost room behind the curtain. Under the law only the high priest entered it, once a year on the Day of Atonement, carrying sacrificial blood. The author applies this to the heavenly presence of God, now open to all worshippers.

verse.text: an entry he inaugurated for us as a new and living way through the curtain, that is, his flesh,
verse.note: Grammatically 'his flesh' most naturally explains 'the curtain', so that Jesus' body, given in death, is what was passed through to open the way. Some interpreters instead attach it to 'way' (the new and living way consisting in his flesh), finding it awkward to compare his body to a barrier. The rendering leaves the phrase where the Greek has it; the first reading is the majority view.

verse.text: and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for the one who promised is faithful.
And let us pay attention to one another, to stir up love and good works,
not abandoning our own meeting together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.
For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,
verse.note: The law distinguished unintentional sins, for which sacrifices were provided, from defiant, 'high-handed' sin, for which there was none (Numbers 15:22–31). The author draws on that distinction. The context (verse 29) shows that he has in view a knowing repudiation of Christ, not every conscious lapse.

verse.text: but a fearful expectation of judgment and the fury of a fire that is about to consume the adversaries.
Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.

How much worse a punishment do you think someone will be judged to deserve who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, treated as profane the blood of the covenant by which he was made holy, and insulted the Spirit of grace?
For we know the one who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” and again, “The Lord will judge his people.”
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
But remember the earlier days, when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard contest of sufferings,
sometimes being made a public spectacle through insults and afflictions, and sometimes becoming partners of those who were treated that way.
For you sympathized with the prisoners and accepted the plundering of your possessions with joy, knowing that you yourselves have a better possession, one that lasts.
verse.note: Some manuscripts read 'my chains' in place of 'the prisoners', which is the reading behind the King James Version and was once used as evidence that Paul wrote the letter. The reading 'the prisoners' is judged original by nearly all modern editors.

verse.text: So do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward.
For you need endurance, so that after doing the will of God you may receive what was promised.
For “yet a very little while, and the one who is coming will come and will not delay;

text.q: but my righteous one will live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul takes no pleasure in him.”

note.term: my righteous one will live by faith
note.traditional: the just shall live by faith

verse.note: Verses 37–38 combine a phrase from Isaiah 26:20 with Habakkuk 2:3–4 in a Greek form, with the clauses reordered so that 'shrinks back' applies to the righteous person. The Greek word translated 'faith' also means 'faithfulness', and in this context of endurance under pressure both senses are in play; the Hebrew of Habakkuk reads 'by his faithfulness'. 'Righteous' and 'just' translate the same Greek word.

verse.text: But we are not of those who shrink back to destruction, but of those who have faith to the preserving of the soul.
Now faith is the reality of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.
verse.note: Most modern versions render this word as an inner state, 'assurance' or 'confidence', paired with 'conviction' for the second term. In the usage of the period the word normally refers to something objective: the underlying reality of a thing, or in legal documents a guarantee of ownership. Its partner term likewise means 'proof' or 'evidence', not a feeling of being convinced. The subjective reading remains common, and the sense here is disputed.

verse.text: For by it the ancients were attested.

note.traditional: were commended; obtained a good report

verse.note: The verb means 'to bear witness', and in the passive 'to have witness borne to one', usually favourably. 'Commended' gives the favourable sense but hides the language of testimony, which recurs in verses 4, 5 and 39 and leads to the 'cloud of witnesses' at the start of the next chapter. The implied witness is God, speaking through Scripture.

verse.text: By faith we understand that the worlds were set in order by God’s word, so that what is seen did not come into being from things that appear.
verse.note: The Greek word is literally 'the ages'. In Jewish Greek the plural could mean the created world in its whole extent of time and space, and the reference to 'what is seen' favours that sense here. Some interpreters keep 'the ages' and take the verse to mean God's ordering of history.

verse.text: By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he was attested as righteous, God attesting to his gifts; and through it, though he died, he still speaks.
By faith Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him away. For it is attested that before he was taken away he had pleased God,
and without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

By faith Noah, warned by God about things not yet seen, in reverent fear built an ark to save his household. Through this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that accords with faith.
By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed and went out to a place he was going to receive as an inheritance; and he went out not knowing where he was going.
By faith he lived as a foreigner in the land of the promise, as in a land belonging to another, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise;
for he was waiting for the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.
By faith, together with Sarah herself, he received power to father offspring, even past the age for it, since he considered the one who had promised faithful.

note.traditional: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts had no accents or iota subscripts, so the words 'Sarah herself' can be read as the subject or as a dative, 'together with Sarah herself'. SBLGNT prints the dative, which makes Abraham the subject. This suits the Greek phrase used, which is the ordinary expression for the father's part in conception, and it suits verse 12, where 'one man' is Abraham. Many translations take Sarah as the subject, and some manuscripts add that she was barren.

verse.text: And so from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of the sky in number and as countless as the sand along the shore of the sea.
All these died in faith, without having received the promises, but having seen them from afar and greeted them, and having confessed that they were strangers and temporary residents on the earth.
For people who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.
And if they had been thinking of the one they had left, they would have had opportunity to return.
But as it is, they long for a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.
By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac. The one who had accepted the promises was offering his one and only son,
verse.note: The word means 'only one of its kind' and was used of an only child; its second element is related to 'kind', not to 'beget'. Isaac was not Abraham's only son, since Ishmael was born first, but he was the unique son through whom the promise ran. 'One and only' is the usual modern rendering, though a minority of scholars have recently defended 'only begotten'.

verse.text: he to whom it had been said, “It is through Isaac that your offspring will be named.”
He reasoned that God is able to raise even from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'in a parable'. It may mean that Isaac's rescue was as good as a return from the dead, or that the event served as a symbol pointing forward, either to resurrection in general or to Christ's. The translation leaves both possibilities open.

verse.text: By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau, even regarding things to come.
By faith Jacob, as he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons, and bowed in worship over the top of his staff.

note.term: over the top of his staff
note.traditional: leaning upon the top of his staff

verse.note: This follows the Greek translation of Genesis 47:31. The Hebrew text as traditionally vocalised says that Jacob bowed at the head of his bed; the same Hebrew consonants can be read as either 'bed' or 'staff'. The author of Hebrews regularly quotes Scripture in its Greek form.

verse.text: By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, spoke of the exodus of the sons of Israel and gave instructions about his bones.
By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict.
By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called a son of Pharaoh’s daughter,
choosing rather to be mistreated along with the people of God than to have the short-lived enjoyment of sin,
considering the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to the reward.
verse.note: The phrase can mean abuse like that which Christ bore, abuse suffered for Christ's sake, or the abuse that falls on God's anointed, here his people. It echoes the language of Psalm 89:50–51, where God's 'anointed' is taunted. The author most likely sees Moses as sharing in advance the disgrace Christ would bear, a theme taken up again at 13:13.

verse.text: By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger, for he persevered as one who sees the unseen one.
By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of the blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them.
By faith they crossed the Red Sea as if over dry land; when the Egyptians tried it, they were swallowed up.
By faith the walls of Jericho fell after being encircled for seven days.
By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who disobeyed, because she had welcomed the spies in peace.
And what more should I say? For time will fail me if I tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets,
who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions,
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. This translation normally uses 'righteous' and 'righteousness', as in verses 4 and 7. Here the list concerns the deeds of judges, kings and prophets, so fair ruling is probably meant, and many modern versions also have 'justice'. 'Did what was right' is also possible.

verse.text: quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made powerful out of weakness, became mighty in war, routed the armies of foreigners.
Women received their dead back by resurrection. Others were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection.
verse.note: The verb refers to a specific instrument of torture on which victims were stretched and beaten to death. The allusion is almost certainly to the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7, the aged scribe Eleazar and seven brothers, who refused to save themselves by breaking the law and declared their hope of resurrection. The 'better resurrection' is contrasted with the return to ordinary life in the first half of the verse.

verse.text: Still others experienced mockery and floggings, and even chains and imprisonment.
They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, mistreated,

note.traditional: they were sawn asunder, were tempted

verse.note: Many manuscripts add 'they were tempted' or 'they were tested' before or after these words, and the King James Version includes it. SBLGNT omits it as a probable scribal addition or duplication of the similar-looking Greek word for 'sawn in two'. Being sawn in two recalls a Jewish tradition about the death of the prophet Isaiah.

verse.text: people of whom the world was not worthy, wandering over deserts and mountains and in caves and holes in the ground.
And all these, though attested through their faith, did not receive the promise,
because God had provided something better with us in view, so that apart from us they would not be brought to completion.
verse.note: The verb means to bring something to its goal or finished state. 'Made perfect' is the traditional rendering throughout Hebrews, but in modern English it suggests flawlessness, whereas the point is that the faithful of earlier times reach the promised goal only together with those who come after. Most translations keep 'made perfect'.

verse.text: Therefore, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, let us too lay aside every weight and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set before us,

keeping our eyes fixed on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured a cross, disregarding its shame, and has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of God.
verse.note: The Greek word covers a leader who goes first, a founder, and an originator. 'Pioneer' fits the picture of a race in which Jesus has already run the course ahead of the runners. 'Author' or 'founder', the older renderings, take the word as 'originator' and are equally defensible.

The Greek has no 'our'. Most translations supply it, making Jesus the one who begins and completes the believer's faith. Without it, the phrase can also present Jesus as the one who himself ran the course of faith from start to finish, the climax of the list of the faithful in chapter 11. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

note.term: for the joy set before him
note.traditional: for the joy that was set before him

verse.note: The preposition can mean 'for the sake of' or 'instead of'. On the first reading, which most interpreters follow, the joy is the reward ahead that made the cross worth enduring. On the second, Jesus chose the cross in place of a joy that was his for the taking. 'For' is used because verse 16 uses the same preposition for an exchange with a view to gain.

verse.text: Consider him who has endured such opposition from sinners against themselves, so that you may not grow weary in your souls and lose heart.
