verse.note: The Greek text translated here has the plural, 'against themselves', which is found in several of the earliest manuscripts. Other manuscripts have the singular, 'against himself', and most English versions follow them. The plural would mean that the sinners' opposition to Jesus was to their own harm, and it may echo the Septuagint's description of Korah's company in Numbers 16.

verse.text: You have not yet resisted to the point of blood in your struggle against sin,
and you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: “My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, nor lose heart when you are corrected by him;

text.q: for the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and flogs every son he accepts.”

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for whipping, and it is the word the Septuagint uses in Proverbs 3:12, which is quoted here. The Hebrew of that verse reads differently ('as a father the son in whom he delights'). 'Chastises' softens a word that a first-century reader would have heard as physical punishment, used here as a picture of painful correction.

verse.text: It is for discipline that you are enduring. God is treating you as sons; for what son is there whom a father does not discipline?

note.term: It is for discipline that you are enduring

verse.note: The verb form can be a statement ('you are enduring') or a command ('endure'). Many translations take it as a command. The statement fits the explanation that follows, in which the author interprets what the readers are already going through.

verse.text: But if you are without the discipline in which all have come to share, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.
Besides, we had the fathers of our flesh to discipline us, and we respected them. Shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live?
For they disciplined us for a few days as seemed good to them, but he does so for our benefit, so that we may share in his holiness.
All discipline seems for the moment to be a matter not of joy but of grief; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice' translate the same Greek words. Here the word refers to a life of doing what is right, the harvest that discipline produces.

verse.text: Therefore straighten the slack hands and the weakened knees,
and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.
verse.note: The verb normally means 'turn aside', which would give 'so that the lame may not stray from the path'. In medical writers it can describe a limb being dislocated, and the contrast with 'be healed' favours that sense here. Either reading is possible.

verse.text: Pursue peace with everyone, and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord,
watching that no one falls short of the grace of God, that no root of bitterness sprouts up and causes trouble, and through it many are defiled,
that no one is sexually immoral or profane like Esau, who for a single meal sold his own rights as firstborn.
For you know that afterward too, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no room for turning back, though he sought it with tears.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'repentance', which most translations keep and which readers generally take to include a change of life. The Greek word denotes a change of course rather than a feeling of sorrow, and 'turning back' reflects that. It is disputed whether the author means that Esau found no way to repent, or that he found no way to get the decision reversed (see Genesis 27:30–40). 'No room for turning back' allows both.

'It' may refer to the blessing or to the turning back; both nouns are feminine in Greek and the pronoun fits either. In Genesis 27 Esau weeps and begs for the blessing, which favours the first. The second is closer in the sentence.

verse.text: For you have not come to what can be touched, to blazing fire and darkness and gloom and storm,

note.traditional: the mount that might be touched

verse.note: Many manuscripts add 'mountain' here, probably drawn from verse 22, and many translations include it. The earliest witnesses lack it, and the text translated here follows them. The scene is Mount Sinai at the giving of the law (Exodus 19; Deuteronomy 4). The words could also be construed as 'a fire that can be touched and is burning'.

verse.text: and the blast of a trumpet and a voice speaking words, a voice whose hearers begged that no further word be spoken to them;
for they could not bear the command: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”
And so fearsome was the sight that Moses said, “I am full of fear and trembling.”
But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, to a festal gathering

note.traditional: to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly

verse.note: The word means a festival crowd, and it can attach to what precedes ('myriads of angels in festal gathering') or to what follows ('a festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn'). The punctuation of the Greek edition translated here joins it to what follows. Many translations take it with the angels.

verse.text: and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in the heavens, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'church', which is near-universal. A first-century reader knew this word as the term for a civic assembly and as the Septuagint's word for Israel gathered before God, as at Sinai, the scene just described. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' keeps the picture of a people gathered.

verse.text: and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks something better than Abel.

See that you do not refuse the one who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused the one who warned them on earth, much less shall we escape if we turn away from the one who warns from the heavens.
His voice shook the earth then, but now he has promised: “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heaven.”
Now this “Yet once more” points to the removal of the things that are shaken, as things that have been made, so that the things that are not shaken may remain.
Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be thankful, and through this let us worship God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and awe,
verse.note: The Greek phrase is literally 'let us have grace', and older translations render it so, meaning 'let us hold on to God's grace'. But 'to have grace' was a common idiom for 'to be grateful', and most modern translations take it that way here.

verse.text: for indeed our God is a consuming fire.
Let brotherly love remain.
Do not forget hospitality to strangers, for through it some have hosted angels without knowing it.
verse.note: The allusion is to Abraham and Lot, who welcomed travellers who turned out to be divine messengers (Genesis 18–19). The Greek plays on two related verbs, “forget” and “escape notice”, and pairs “love of brothers” (v. 1) with “love of strangers” (hospitality).

verse.text: Remember the prisoners as though imprisoned with them, and those who are mistreated, since you yourselves are also in a body.
Let marriage be held in honor by all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.

note.term: Let marriage be held in honor by all

verse.note: The Greek has no verb. Most modern translations supply a command, as here, because the surrounding sentences are exhortations; older versions read it as a statement (“marriage is honourable”). The phrase rendered “by all” could also mean “in every respect”.

verse.text: Keep your way of life free from the love of money, and be content with what you have, for he himself has said, “I will never leave you, and I will never abandon you.”
So we can say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can a human being do to me?”
Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their conduct, and imitate their faith.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever.
Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be made firm by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those who live by them.
verse.note: What teaching about food is meant is disputed. Most scholars think of Jewish food regulations or sacred meals linked to sacrifice, in line with the letter's earlier remark about rules of food and drink (9:10); the argument in verses 10–12 moves straight to the altar and its offerings.

verse.text: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent and here means the tent-sanctuary Israel carried in the wilderness. “Tabernacle” is the traditional English term, and several modern translations already use “tent”. Hebrews argues from the wilderness tent as described in the Law throughout, not from the Jerusalem temple.

verse.text: For the bodies of the animals whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest as an offering for sin are burned outside the camp.
verse.note: On the Day of Atonement the high priest carried the blood of the sin offerings into the inner sanctuary, and the carcasses were not eaten but burned outside Israel's camp (Leviticus 16:27). The author sees this matched in Jesus' execution outside the city gate (v. 12). “As an offering for sin” renders the Septuagint's set phrase for the sin offering, literally “concerning sin”.

verse.text: So Jesus also suffered outside the gate, in order to make the people holy through his own blood.
So then, let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing the abuse he bore.
For here we have no city that remains, but we are seeking the one that is to come.
Through him, then, let us continually offer up to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name.

note.traditional: giving thanks to his name; confess his name

verse.note: The verb normally means to declare or acknowledge openly. With “to his name” it may instead echo the Septuagint idiom for praising or giving thanks to God's name, which would suit “sacrifice of praise”. “Fruit of lips” is itself a Septuagint phrase (Hosea 14:2).

verse.text: And do not forget to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.

Obey your leaders and yield to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who will give an account, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.
verse.note: The verb's basic sense is “be persuaded”. With a person as its object it regularly meant to comply with or obey them, and the traditional rendering is kept. Some interpreters prefer “trust” or “be persuaded by”, stressing willing assent. The same verb appears in verse 18 as “we are convinced”.

verse.text: Pray for us, for we are convinced that we have a good conscience, wanting to conduct ourselves well in everything.
I exhort you all the more to do this, so that I may be restored to you sooner.
Now may the God of peace, who brought up from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep by the blood of an eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus,
equip you with every good thing to do his will, working in us what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between “in us” and “in you”; the two Greek pronouns differ by one letter and were pronounced alike. The SBLGNT reads “us”, which is followed here.

verse.text: I exhort you, brothers and sisters, bear with this word of exhortation, for I have written to you only briefly.
verse.note: The plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and the letter is written to the whole community. Many modern translations render it this way, while others keep “brothers”. The same root lies behind “brotherly love” in verse 1.

The same phrase is used in Acts 13:15 for an address given in the synagogue after the Scripture readings, so the author is probably describing the whole work as a sermon sent in writing. The noun covers both urging and encouragement, and the verb “I exhort” is from the same root.

verse.text: Know that our brother Timothy has been released. If he comes soon, I will see you with him.
verse.note: Most take this to mean release from custody, though no imprisonment of Timothy is recorded elsewhere. The verb can also mean “sent off” or “departed”, so it may only say that he has set out. “Know” could also be read as a statement: “you know”.

verse.text: Greet all your leaders and all the holy ones. Those from Italy greet you.
verse.note: “Saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”, and others use “God's people”.

The phrase can mean people who are in Italy, which would make Italy the place of writing, or Italians living elsewhere who send greetings home, which would make Italy the destination. The Greek does not settle it, and scholars are divided.

verse.text: Grace be with you all.
